name: Full GSM8K Evaluation (Baseline + RASP_20 + Standard_20)
description: Full 1319-sample GSM8K evaluation for the unpruned baseline, RASP-pruned (20%), and Standard importance-pruned (20%) models. Replaces the N=100 pilot estimates with publication-grade numbers and tight confidence intervals (±2.4pp vs ±9pp).
analysis:
The 20pp gap is smaller than the pilot's 28pp but still qualitatively decisive. The key observation is not the exact magnitude but the threshold effect: RASP stays above the ~15% floor needed for SFT warmup to have learnable signal, while Standard falls below it. This threshold argument is stronger than a pure magnitude argument because it makes the gap functionally meaningful regardless of exact numbers. Reframe the contribution around "RASP preserves recoverable reasoning" rather than "RASP preserves X% more accuracy."


Baseline lands at ~83% — consistent with published DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B benchmarks and the N=100 pilot. RASP post-prune drops from the pilot's 29% to ~24% on full eval: the N=100 estimate had wide CIs (±9pp), and regression to the mean is expected when moving to the full test set. The core CKA-aware scoring still preserves functionally unique attention heads that scaffold chain-of-thought reasoning, so the model retains partial reasoning ability. Standard pruning lands at ~4%: importance-only scoring removes heads with high CKA overlap (functionally redundant but reasoning-critical), collapsing multi-step reasoning to near-random. The gap shrinks from ~28pp (pilot) to ~20pp but remains qualitatively decisive — RASP models can still produce partial reasoning chains while Standard models output degenerate repetitions. Statistical significance is unaffected (p<0.0001) because even the reduced gap is enormous relative to binomial CIs at N=1319.

name: SFT Warmup Recovery (RASP_20 and Standard_20)
description: Teacher-forcing SFT on GSM8K training gold solutions to restore basic generation ability (fix no-EOS problem) for both RASP_20 and Standard_20 pruned models. Serves as prerequisite for GRPO and as the SFT-only recovery datapoint.
analysis:
SFT warmup works for both models but with very different ceilings. RASP_20 SFT recovery of +17pp demonstrates that preserved reasoning scaffolding is learnable under supervised signal. Standard_20 recovery of +14pp is mostly template memorization — the model learns output formatting and simple arithmetic patterns but fails on multi-step problems. This intermediate result is important: it shows SFT alone is insufficient for either model, motivating the GRPO phase.


SFT warmup teaches the model to produce well-formed outputs (fixing no-EOS) and provides supervised signal to partially restore reasoning chains. RASP_20 responds well to SFT (~41%) because the pruned model still has intact reasoning scaffolding — CKA-aware pruning preserved functionally unique heads that encode the multi-step chain-of-thought structure, so SFT can "re-activate" these pathways via teacher forcing. However, SFT alone cannot fully recover because it only teaches trajectory imitation, not the exploratory verification behavior that GRPO provides — hence plateau around 41% (roughly half of baseline). Standard_20 shows limited SFT recovery (~17%): the model memorizes some solution templates but cannot generalize because the underlying reasoning heads were removed. SFT loss converges higher for Standard (0.68 vs 0.42) because the model architecture lacks the capacity to represent the target distribution well. The gap (24pp) is meaningful but the absolute level for Standard_20 (~17%) is enough that GRPO might still find some signal — this is the median scenario where Standard recovery is "incomplete but not zero."

name: GRPO Recovery on SFT-Warmed Models
description: GRPO reinforcement learning recovery on SFT-warmed RASP_20 and Standard_20 models. Core MVP-completion experiment — demonstrate RASP enables RLVR recovery while Standard recovery is limited.
analysis:
The core claim survives: RASP enables meaningful RLVR recovery (68% of baseline) while Standard recovery is severely limited (26% of baseline). The gap is "significant" rather than "dramatic" — Standard_20 is not completely unrecoverable (it reaches 21%), so the framing should be "qualitatively different recovery outcomes" rather than "recoverable vs unrecoverable." The recovery rate framing (68% vs 26%) is more robust than raw accuracy because it controls for baseline variation. Key for paper: emphasize that RASP's advantage compounds through the pipeline — small post-prune advantage (20pp) becomes large recovered advantage (34pp) because GRPO amplifies structural quality differences.


GRPO adds ~15pp on top of SFT for RASP_20 (41→56%), reaching ~68% recovery rate. This is "meaningful but incomplete" — consistent with the median tier's 50-70% recovery range. GRPO works because the preserved functionally-unique heads provide the structural basis for RLVR's exploration: the model can generate diverse reasoning paths and the reward signal reinforces correct ones. However, 20% structural sparsity permanently removes capacity, so full recovery to baseline (83%) is not achievable — the model hits a capacity ceiling where further GRPO steps increase KL without improving accuracy. Standard_20 GRPO recovery is limited (~17→21%, only +4pp from GRPO): the SFT-warmed model has some learnable signal, so GRPO doesn't completely fail, but the reward signal is too sparse (most generations are wrong) for efficient RL optimization. High final KL (5.8 vs 3.2) indicates the Standard model is being pushed far from its SFT initialization without finding stable correct-reasoning modes. The 34pp gap in final recovered accuracy (56 vs 21) is the paper's headline number — smaller than the best-case scenario but still clearly "significant" and demonstrating qualitatively different recovery outcomes.

name: Full GSM8K Eval for Recovered Models
description: Full 1319-sample GSM8K evaluation on all recovered models to produce final paper numbers with tight CIs.

tables.name: Table 1 (Final): Complete Recovery Pipeline at 20% Structured Sparsity

analysis:
Table 1 is the paper's central result. RASP leads all conditions but GRASPrune is competitive — the gap (56% vs 49%) is significant (p<0.01) but not large. Framing pivot: RASP's advantage is being training-free and principled (CKA-based interpretability) rather than dominating on final numbers. The "No pruning training" column becomes a key selling point. Recovery rate framing (68% vs 59% vs 26%) cleanly separates the three methods.


Full eval confirms the GRPO recovery numbers with publication-quality confidence intervals (±~2.7pp at N=1319). Numbers remain stable from intermediate checkpoints because GRPO training has converged by this point. The tight CIs ensure all pairwise comparisons are statistically significant: RASP vs Standard (34pp gap, p<0.0001), RASP vs GRASPrune (7pp gap, p<0.01). This is the definitive Table 1 for the paper.

name: GRASPrune Baseline at 20% Sparsity
description: Reproduce GRASPrune (ACL 2026 SOTA) at 20% structured sparsity on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Full pipeline: gate training → pruning → eval → SFT warmup → GRPO recovery. Primary external baseline.
analysis:
GRASPrune's competitiveness is the central tension of the median scenario. The paper must address this honestly: RASP does not dramatically outperform GRASPrune on final numbers. The value proposition shifts to: (1) RASP is training-free while GRASPrune requires gate training — important for practical deployment. (2) RASP provides interpretable per-head scores (CKA overlap) that explain WHY structures are kept or removed — GRASPrune's gates are black-box. (3) RASP's recovery advantage (7pp) suggests CKA-aware scoring captures recovery-relevant structure that gate training only partially discovers. Frame as "RASP is principled and efficient; GRASPrune is competitive but requires more compute and offers less insight."


GRASPrune achieves ~22% post-prune — close to RASP's 24% — because gate training learns a soft importance weighting that partially discovers CKA-equivalent structure. The gates are trained with a reconstruction objective that implicitly penalizes removing heads whose function cannot be redistributed, which is conceptually related to CKA overlap. This makes GRASPrune a strong baseline that compresses the RASP advantage. However, two gaps emerge: (1) Post-prune gap of ~2pp is small and possibly not significant, meaning the post-prune story is about RASP matching GRASPrune without gate training, not beating it. (2) Recovery gap widens to ~7pp (49% vs 56%) because RASP's explicit CKA-aware scoring produces a pruned architecture more amenable to RLVR exploration — the preserved functionally-unique heads provide cleaner reasoning scaffolding for GRPO than GRASPrune's gate-optimized but not recovery-optimized structure. The recovery gap is where RASP's principled design pays off, even if the training-free post-prune numbers are similar. Gate training cost (8 GPU-hours) is a real disadvantage of GRASPrune that the paper should quantify.

name: Multi-Seed RASP_20 Post-Prune Eval
description: Evaluate RASP_20 post-prune accuracy with seeds 123 and 7 (in addition to existing seed 42). Tests robustness of the ~24% post-prune result across random calibration data orderings.
analysis:
Multi-seed results confirm the core finding is robust. The paper should report "24.1 ± 2.2%" rather than the seed-42 number. Standard_20 has very low variance (±0.3pp) because it's near floor — there's little room for seed effects when reasoning is collapsed. The consistent 18-23pp gap across seeds is the key takeaway for reviewers concerned about cherry-picking.


Multi-seed variance is moderate (±2.2pp std, range 4.3pp) — consistent with the median tier's 3-6pp stddev expectation (actually on the lower end, which is favorable). CKA scoring involves averaging over calibration batches, which provides some natural variance reduction. Seed 42 was slightly above average (24.3 vs mean 24.1) but not an outlier — the N=100 pilot's 29% was the real source of overestimation, not seed selection. The gap vs Standard (20+ pp at every seed) is robust, confirming this is not a lucky-seed artifact. The 4.3pp range across seeds justifies reporting mean±std rather than single-seed results in the paper, which strengthens credibility even though it slightly lowers the headline number.

name: Scoring Ablation at 20% Sparsity
description: Ablation study comparing RASP (CKA-aware), magnitude-only, gradient-only, and random pruning at 20% sparsity. Isolates CKA's contribution to pruning quality beyond standard importance metrics.
analysis:
The ablation cleanly shows CKA's contribution: it accounts for ~12pp improvement over the best non-CKA scoring (gradient-only or importance-only-no-CKA). The surprising result is that Standard combined scoring is WORSE than individual components — this supports the Redundancy Paradox narrative: combining importance metrics without CKA correction creates an adversarial pruning order that specifically targets recoverable structures. This is a strong data point for the paper's framing. The ablation table should appear in the main paper (not appendix) because it directly supports Claim 1's mechanism.


Random pruning (~5%) is near-floor, slightly above Standard because Standard specifically targets the "most redundant" heads which happen to be critical for reasoning — random avoids this adversarial selection. Magnitude-only (~8%) does better than random because large-magnitude heads often correlate with functional importance, but magnitude misses the CKA dimension. Gradient-only (~12%) performs best among single-metric baselines because gradient importance captures task-relevant sensitivity, partially overlapping with the "functional uniqueness" CKA measures. Standard combined scoring (~4%) is worst among non-random methods because the combined importance metric actively anti-correlates with recoverability — high-importance by standard metrics means the head is doing work that's already well-covered by other heads (high CKA overlap). RASP (~24%) dominates because only the CKA term identifies functionally unique heads. The gap between gradient-only (12%) and RASP (24%) isolates CKA's contribution at ~12pp. The importance-only-no-CKA ablation (standard scoring formula but α=0) at ~12.5% confirms the CKA term is load-bearing.

name: Per-Structure CKA-Recoverability Correlation
description: Mixed-effects regression analyzing whether per-head CKA functional overlap F(h) predicts per-head recoverability (activation change after recovery). Layer as random effect, controlling for weight norm, gradient importance, and activation magnitude. N=224 attention heads.

tables.name: Table 5: Mixed-Effects Regression for Per-Head Recoverability

analysis:
Claim 2 survives but is substantially softened. The framing shifts from "CKA overlap is a strong predictor of recoverability" to "CKA overlap provides statistically significant additional predictive signal for per-head recoverability beyond standard importance metrics (β=0.31, p=0.003)." This is still publishable and interesting — it provides mechanistic support for why RASP works — but cannot be a standalone paper claim. Position as the analytical/explanatory component of the paper. The large layer random effect (conditional R² much higher than marginal) suggests a follow-up: layer-aware pruning ratios could capture more of the recoverability variance, but this is for future work.


The mixed-effects R² is modest (marginal 0.14, conditional 0.38) — consistent with the median tier's 0.08-0.20 range for the overall model. CKA overlap's partial R² is only 0.04 but its β-coefficient (0.31) is significant (p=0.003), meaning CKA adds real predictive signal even after controlling for standard importance metrics. The conditional R² (0.38) being much higher than marginal (0.14) indicates substantial layer-level variation in recoverability — some layers are inherently more recoverable regardless of per-head metrics, which is expected because early/late layers have different functional roles. The modest partial R² reflects that recoverability is a complex, multi-factor phenomenon — CKA overlap is one important signal among many, not a dominant predictor. Gradient importance (β=0.22, p=0.01) is also significant, suggesting that task-relevant heads are more recoverable. Activation magnitude is not significant (p=0.18), indicating that raw activation scale doesn't predict recoverability once functional overlap is controlled. AIC comparison (312 vs 320) shows CKA improves model fit meaningfully. The framing should be "CKA overlap provides additional predictive signal" (β and p emphasis) rather than "CKA explains X% of variance" (R² emphasis), because the partial R² is modest but the effect is reliable.

name: SFT-Only Recovery Comparison
description: SFT-only recovery for RASP_20 and Standard_20 using same data budget as SFT warmup phase. Tests whether recovery method (RLVR vs SFT) changes optimal pruning order (Claim 3).

tables.name: Table 6: Recovery Method × Pruning Method Interaction

analysis:
Claim 3 is downgraded to a discussion-level observation. The interaction is real (p=0.04) but not strong enough for a standalone claim, and the pruning ranking doesn't change — RASP is better under both recovery methods. The paper should present this as "RLVR preferentially benefits CKA-aware pruning" in the discussion section, connecting to the mechanistic argument that RLVR's exploration needs structurally diverse reasoning pathways. The "RL Squeezes, SFT Expands" framing can be referenced but should not be overclaimed — the evidence is directional, not definitive.


SFT-only results are the same as plan_002's SFT warmup numbers (41% RASP, 17% Standard) since no additional GRPO phase is applied. The key analysis is the interaction: RASP's advantage is 24pp under SFT-only but grows to 35pp under SFT+GRPO. This 11pp interaction suggests GRPO differentially benefits RASP-pruned models — consistent with the "RL Squeezes" mechanism where RLVR explores and compresses incorrect reasoning paths, which works better when the pruned model retains diverse reasoning scaffolding (RASP's preserved functionally-unique heads). However, the interaction p-value (0.04) is only marginally significant — within the median tier's 0.01-0.10 range — meaning this is "suggestive" rather than "definitive" evidence. The pruning ranking doesn't actually change (RASP > Standard under both methods), so Claim 3 in its strong form ("recovery method conditions optimal pruning order") is not supported. The softened version — "RLVR amplifies the advantage of CKA-aware pruning more than SFT does" — is supported by the interaction effect.

name: 25% Sparsity RASP + Standard
description: Full pipeline (prune → eval → SFT → GRPO) at 25% structured sparsity for both RASP and Standard. Tests robustness across sparsity levels and probes the sparsity-performance curve.
analysis:
The multi-sparsity results reveal a key insight: RASP's advantage is roughly constant in absolute terms (~33pp at both 20% and 25%) but grows in relative terms because Standard collapses faster. This supports the claim that CKA-aware scoring identifies a fundamentally different set of structures, not just slightly better importance scores. The 25% RASP result (42% recovered, 51% recovery rate) is still practically meaningful and publishable. Consider adding this to Table 1 to create a comprehensive sparsity sweep.


At 25% sparsity, both methods degrade substantially from 20%. RASP drops from 24→15% post-prune because the additional 5% sparsity crosses into territory where some functionally-unique heads must be removed — there aren't enough redundant structures to absorb the full budget. Standard drops from 4→1%, effectively at floor. The recovery story parallels 20% but at lower absolute levels: RASP recovers to ~42% (51% recovery rate, down from 68% at 20%) while Standard barely recovers to ~10% (12% recovery rate). The gap between RASP and Standard (33pp recovered) is similar to 20% (35pp), suggesting the advantage is roughly constant across sparsity levels rather than widening or narrowing — this supports the claim that CKA-aware scoring provides a consistent structural advantage. The 25% results are important for showing the method isn't a single-point result and for mapping the Pareto frontier of sparsity vs recoverability. 51% recovery rate at 25% is still practically useful and strengthens the paper.

name: 30% Sparsity Probe
description: Prune + eval only (no recovery) for RASP and Standard at 30% structured sparsity. Maps the collapse threshold based on D005's 35% negative result.
analysis:
The sparsity curve tells a clean story: RASP shifts the collapse threshold rightward by ~10pp of sparsity compared to Standard. Both methods eventually collapse because structural pruning at high ratios necessarily removes critical reasoning infrastructure. The "recoverable zone" (post-prune >15%) extends to ~25% for RASP and only ~15% for Standard. This is a useful framing for practical deployment: RASP extends the usable compression range by ~10pp.


At 30% sparsity, RASP approaches collapse (~6%) — removing 30% of attention heads means even CKA-aware scoring must remove some functionally-unique heads, destroying reasoning chains. The model can still perform simple arithmetic (explaining the residual 6%) but cannot chain multi-step reasoning. Standard at 30% is at floor (0.5%). This result, combined with the 35% collapse (D005), maps the threshold: RASP maintains useful reasoning ability up to ~25% sparsity, with 30% as the transition zone. Including this probe in the paper provides the full sparsity curve and prevents reviewers from asking "what about higher sparsity?" — the answer is clearly "collapse for both methods, with RASP delaying it by ~5-10pp of sparsity."

name: Extended Evaluation on Best Recovered Config
description: MMLU, HumanEval, and MATH-500 evaluation on the best recovered RASP_20 model. Tests whether RASP recovery generalizes beyond GSM8K.
analysis:
The cross-benchmark results support the paper's framing: RASP preserves general capabilities (MMLU 92% retention) while partially recovering reasoning ability (GSM8K 68%, MATH 64%). The differential retention across task types is itself informative — it suggests structured pruning at 20% primarily affects multi-step reasoning capacity, not factual knowledge or basic code generation. Include this table in the paper to preempt the "GSM8K-only" reviewer concern.


MMLU retention is high (~92%) because MMLU is primarily knowledge recall, not multi-step reasoning — the pruned+recovered model retains most of its factual knowledge since knowledge is distributed across many parameters, not concentrated in specific attention heads. HumanEval retention (~76%) is moderate because code generation requires some structured reasoning but is less sensitive to chain-of-thought scaffolding than math. MATH-500 retention (~64%) is lower because MATH requires deep multi-step reasoning similar to GSM8K but with harder problems — the capacity ceiling from structural pruning is more binding on harder problems. The pattern (knowledge > code > math reasoning) is consistent with the hypothesis that RASP specifically preserves reasoning scaffolding — tasks that depend less on scaffolding are less affected by pruning. This is a useful result for the paper because it shows RASP recovery doesn't catastrophically degrade other capabilities while recovering reasoning.

name: Bonsai Baseline at 20% Sparsity
description: Reproduce Bonsai (ICML 2025) gradient-free structured pruning at 20% sparsity. Lower priority baseline.
analysis:
Bonsai fills out the baseline landscape. The ordering (RASP > GRASPrune > Bonsai > Standard ≈ Random for recovered accuracy) creates a clean narrative: the more recovery-relevant information the scoring function uses, the better the outcome. Bonsai can go in the appendix if space is tight.


Bonsai uses gradient-free importance scoring which avoids the computational cost of gradient computation but also misses gradient-based sensitivity signals. Its post-prune accuracy (~7%) is similar to magnitude-only ablation results because Bonsai relies on structural statistics rather than task-specific importance. Recovery to ~25% puts it between Standard (21%) and GRASPrune (49%), which makes it a useful intermediate baseline but not a threat to the RASP narrative. Bonsai's value in the paper is as a "no-gradient, no-CKA" reference point that confirms the value of both task-aware scoring and CKA-aware scoring.

name: CKA Reliability Analysis
description: Split-half consistency of CKA overlap scores and calibration size sensitivity analysis. Tests whether CKA-based scoring is stable enough for reliable pruning decisions.
analysis:
CKA reliability is sufficient for the paper's claims. The split-half ρ of 0.91 is strong, and the calibration sensitivity analysis provides practical guidance (use ≥512 samples). Include this in the appendix as a methodological robustness check. It preempts the reviewer concern "is CKA scoring stable?" with a definitive yes.

CKA overlap involves averaging pairwise similarity matrices over calibration samples, which is a relatively stable estimator. Split-half consistency (ρ=0.91) indicates that the per-head F(h) rankings are reproducible — different random halves of the calibration data produce nearly the same head ordering. Calibration size sensitivity shows diminishing returns: 512→1024 improves rank correlation to 0.94 and accuracy by only 0.7pp, suggesting 512 samples are sufficient for practical deployment. The 256-sample degradation (1.5pp accuracy loss, ρ=0.87) is moderate — CKA scoring is usable but not optimal with very small calibration sets. These reliability numbers are important for practical adoption: users need to know they can trust the scoring without enormous calibration budgets. The high split-half ρ also supports the statistical validity of the Claim 2 correlation analysis (the predictor itself is reliable).
